mcqs.question: Why does RecyclerView's ViewHolder cache findViewById results at construction time rather than looking them up fresh on every bind?
options: findViewById cannot be called more than once per view in Android
Caching is required by the RecyclerView API and will crash if omitted

findViewById performs a tree walk to locate a child view, which is real work — caching it once per ViewHolder instance turns a per-bind cost into a one-time cost per recycled view, not per row of data ever displayed
It has no performance benefit; it's purely a code-style convention
mcqs.explanation: findViewById walks the view hierarchy to find a child by ID, and onBindViewHolder runs on every scroll-triggered rebind — caching the lookup once at construction avoids repeating that tree walk on every single bind, which is a meaningful cost difference over a long scrolling session.

mcqs.question: Why should expensive setup work go in onCreateViewHolder rather than onBindViewHolder?
options: onCreateViewHolder runs rarely — only when the recycled pool needs a genuinely new instance — while onBindViewHolder runs frequently, on every scroll-triggered rebind, so expensive work there directly costs scroll performance
onBindViewHolder cannot contain any code beyond setting text values
onCreateViewHolder runs on a background thread automatically
There's no meaningful difference in call frequency between the two methods
mcqs.explanation: onCreateViewHolder is called only when the pool needs to inflate a new view instance, which happens rarely relative to scrolling, while onBindViewHolder runs on every single rebind during a scroll — putting expensive work in the frequently-called method directly costs scroll smoothness.

mcqs.question: A list has one item updated out of a thousand. What does DiffUtil provide that a full adapter refresh doesn't?
options: It computes the minimal set of changes (in this case, one changed item) and dispatches only that targeted update, avoiding a rebind of every visible row and preserving scroll position and animations
DiffUtil eliminates the need for a RecyclerView.Adapter entirely
DiffUtil only works when items are added, never when they're changed or removed
It automatically fetches the updated data from the network
mcqs.explanation: DiffUtil compares old and new lists and computes exactly which operations (insert/remove/move/change) actually occurred, letting the adapter dispatch only those specific updates — this avoids the unnecessary rebinds, animation resets, and scroll-position jumps a full refresh causes for what should be a single-row change.

mcqs.question: A paginated list triggers its next-page fetch only when the user scrolls to the literal last visible item. What's the UX consequence?
options: No consequence — this is the recommended trigger point for pagination
This approach loads the entire dataset upfront, defeating pagination entirely
This causes duplicate requests to fire on every scroll frame
The user will almost always see a visible loading stutter, since the network request hasn't even started until they're already at the point where they need the data
mcqs.explanation: Waiting until the user reaches the literal last item means the fetch starts exactly when there's no more buffer to hide its latency, guaranteeing a visible stutter — triggering the fetch a threshold of items earlier gives the network round trip a head start so it often finishes before the user actually needs it.

mcqs.question: A single row's data changes and the code calls notifyDataSetChanged() to reflect it. What's the downside compared to a targeted update?
options: notifyDataSetChanged() will throw an exception if called more than once per session

It forces every currently visible ViewHolder to rebind regardless of whether its data actually changed, and can visibly reset scroll position or in-progress animations, since the adapter has no information about what specifically changed
There is no real downside; both approaches perform identically
notifyDataSetChanged() only works correctly with lists smaller than 100 items
mcqs.explanation: notifyDataSetChanged() tells the adapter to treat the update as a full, unstructured refresh, forcing every visible row to rebind even when only one item changed — a targeted notifyItemChanged or a DiffUtil-computed update avoids the unnecessary rebinds and the visible scroll/animation glitches a full refresh can cause.

mcqs.question: An async image load started in onBindViewHolder completes after that ViewHolder has already been recycled and rebound with a different item's data. What goes wrong if the load isn't cancelled on recycle?
options: The app crashes immediately
The image loading library automatically discards any load older than one second
Nothing goes wrong; the image simply fails to load silently

The old image can render into what is now a completely different row, since the ViewHolder view is the same object but now displaying different data — a visible correctness bug, not just a performance issue
mcqs.explanation: Because ViewHolder views are reused across different data, an async load that isn't cancelled when its ViewHolder gets recycled can complete late and render its result into a row that's since been rebound to different data — proper image-loading libraries handle this cancellation automatically, but a hand-rolled load has to explicitly account for it.
